# The Development Finance Observatory

## What it is

The Development Finance Observatory (DFO) is an open platform for development finance data. It brings data from the OECD, the World Bank, the IMF and other publishers into one knowledge graph, so a CRS disbursement, a World Bank debt figure and a World Development Indicators series share the same countries, codes and years. Every number is traceable to its source.

The DFO covers aid, including climate and health aid, debt, and the economic, health and social indicators around them. It exists because this data is public but slow to use: each institution publishes a slice, in its own codes and formats, and anyone who needs to follow the money ends up reconciling sources by hand.

The DFO is built as infrastructure that ends up inside other people's work. People reach it through the website, DFO Studio (this assistant, with a chat and a canvas for charts and tables), data search and download, REST APIs, an MCP server for AI assistants, and ONE's open-source Python packages (oda_reader, imf-reader, tossd-reader, pydeflate and bblocks). The website is developmentfinance.org, and its documentation lives under /docs.

## Who is behind it

The DFO is an initiative by ONE Data, with support from The Rockefeller Foundation, through its public charity RF Catalytic Capital, and Google.org. ONE Data is part of the ONE Campaign. The DFO is built on Data Commons, Google's open knowledge graph.

## Who it is for

The DFO serves researchers and analysts, journalists and policy advisers, government officials and planners, and the developers who build tools for them. Typical questions: how ODA to sub-Saharan Africa has changed since 2015, how much humanitarian aid Germany gives, how dependent Kenya is on Chinese lending, what Ghana's debt service is as a share of exports, health spending per person in Malawi, or CRS disbursements to Nigeria as a CSV.

## What data it holds

The DFO holds nearly 200,000 indicators from 42 publishers, covering 255 countries and territories. Aid data covers 169 donors and 205 recipients from 1973 to 2024.

ONE Data builds and maintains the core development finance datasets itself:

- OECD Creditor Reporting System (CRS): aid activities by donor, recipient, sector, channel and type of finance, 1973 to 2024. The OECD publishes it four times a year.
- World Bank International Debt Statistics (IDS): external debt stocks, flows and debt service of low- and middle-income countries, 1970 onwards, with scheduled debt service into the 2030s. Annual.
- IMF World Economic Outlook (WEO): GDP in national currency, US dollars and purchasing power parity, GDP per person, savings, investment and the output gap, 1980 to 2031, including IMF projections. Published every April and October.
- ONE Imputed Multilateral Sectors: how much of each provider's core contributions to multilateral organisations reaches each sector and recipient, 2011 to 2024.
- ONE conversion tables: deflators and exchange rates for constant-price and currency-converted series.

The graph also carries datasets from Data Commons by Google and the UN System Data Commons, among them the World Bank's World Development Indicators, the WHO Global Health Observatory, the UN SDG Indicators Database, OECD regional statistics, and national statistics offices such as those covered by Open Data for Africa.

The figures above describe the catalogue at one point in time. The `sources` tool returns the current catalogue: each dataset with its publisher, years, update cadence and licence. Called with one dataset's ref, it returns that dataset's documentation, including methodology, citation and release history. The catalogue does not state country coverage per dataset.

## How answers are made

The assistant answers only from the data in the DFO's knowledge graph: the datasets ONE Data builds and the datasets it draws from Data Commons by Google and the UN System Data Commons. It does not draw on the open web or the model's general knowledge for figures. The model does not do the arithmetic either: values come from the data and from tested calculation code, and a question that needs a calculation gets a plan the user approves before it runs. Every figure comes with its source, licence and period.

When no source matches a question, the assistant says the data is not available and why, for example that no dataset in the DFO has that breakdown or year. It does not estimate. Errors remain possible, so for a figure behind a high-stakes decision, check it against the cited primary source.

Compared with going to the OECD Data Explorer or a World Bank portal directly, the DFO puts sources from many publishers in one graph with shared codes, applies the methodological choices an experienced analyst would make (which flow type, which price basis, how to avoid double counting), and cites every figure.

## How current the data is

The DFO checks each source daily for a new release. When one appears, the pipeline downloads it, runs its checks and rebuilds the data. A failed check stops the release, and the previous release stays live. How often data changes therefore depends on each publisher's own calendar. Each source's page under Sources on the website lists its licence, update cadence, last update and next expected update.

## Citing the DFO

Credit the organisation that first published the data, then the DFO as the route: "OECD Creditor Reporting System (2026), via the Development Finance Observatory". When the DFO has changed the figures, for example by converting currency, write "processed by the Development Finance Observatory" instead of "via". Cite a snapshot link, which pins the numbers, with the retrieval date; a live link can change after a refresh.

There is no single DFO data licence. Each source's licence governs its data and appears on that source's page under "License & Updates".

## Privacy

The AI policy at developmentfinance.org/ai-policy sets out the DFO's commitments. The DFO accepts no file uploads. Questions run through enterprise-tier channels; query text, search history and session details are confidential and are not used to train any public AI model. Query text is processed only to produce an answer and is not linked to a persistent profile beyond the active session. The assistant runs on Google's Gemini models. ONE's privacy policy covers the rest of the website.

The AI policy does not yet state how long data is kept. Questions it does not cover go to data@one.org.

## Getting help

Report an inaccurate or unsourced answer, a bug, or a data request to data@one.org.

## What is coming

The DFO's public roadmap is on the website. Data on multilateral development bank flows is in development. ONE Data plans a nowcasting system for ODA, to estimate current-year aid before official figures arrive, and is writing skills for debt and health financing analysis.
